title: SharePoint admin prompt: review site sprawl and oversharing from a site inventory export
summary: Turn a SharePoint site inventory export into a ranked cleanup list: inactive sites, missing owners, risky sharing and a safe order of actions for the admin team.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a senior SharePoint Online administrator who runs quarterly governance reviews for a tenant with [number] sites.

Context: I am attaching an export of our site inventory as a table (columns: Site URL, Template, Site owners, Created date, Last activity date, Storage used in GB, Sensitivity label, External sharing setting, Number of guest users). The export comes from [source, for example the SharePoint admin center active sites report or a PowerShell script]. Our rules: every site needs at least two owners, sites without activity for [180] days are archive candidates, and sites with guests need a business justification. Our tenant default for external sharing is [Existing guests only].

Task:
1. Group the sites into four buckets: (a) no or single owner, (b) inactive beyond the threshold, (c) external sharing wider than the default or with many guests, (d) healthy.
2. For every site in buckets a to c, give one recommended action from this list only: assign owners, archive after owner confirmation, reduce sharing, apply a sensitivity label, review guests, no action.
3. Rank the top 15 sites by risk. Explain each ranking in one sentence that cites the values from the table.
4. Propose a safe execution order: what can be done in week 1 without asking anyone, what needs owner confirmation, and what needs a change ticket.

Format: Start with a three-line management summary. Then a table with the columns Site URL, Bucket, Risk (High, Medium, Low), Evidence, Recommended action, Who must approve. End with a list of data gaps you noticed, for example empty owner fields or missing dates, and do not guess values for them.

Rules: Use only the data I provided. If a column is missing, say so instead of inventing numbers. Do not recommend deleting anything; recommend archiving or retention review instead. Mark every assumption with the word Assumption.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Project-Atlas | Team site | jane@contoso.com | 2022-03-14 | 2024-01-09 | 48 | none | Anyone | 0
https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/HR-Policies | Communication site | hr-admins@contoso.com; li@contoso.com | 2021-06-01 | 2025-10-30 | 3 | Confidential | Existing guests only | 2

With this input a good answer flags Project-Atlas for a single owner, long inactivity and the widest sharing setting, and leaves HR-Policies in the healthy bucket while noting the two guests for a justification check.

WHEN TO USE
Use this prompt before a quarterly access review, before a Copilot rollout (oversharing becomes visible quickly once people can search with natural language), or when you inherit a tenant and need a first triage. It works in Copilot Chat with an uploaded file or pasted table, and in Excel if the export is already a table there.

HOW TO ADAPT
Replace the thresholds with your own policy values. If you use hub sites, add a column for the hub and ask for a grouping by hub. If you must respect regional rules, add the column Geo location and ask the model to keep reporting per region. For very large exports, run the prompt per template type (team sites, communication sites) so that the answer stays complete. You can also ask for a PowerShell outline for the approved actions, but always review the script and run it in a test scope first.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Pasting the export without column names. The answer then mixes up owners and guests.
- Letting the model decide the thresholds. Always state them; otherwise the result looks precise but is arbitrary.
- Treating the output as a decision. It is a triage list; owners must confirm before any archive or sharing change.
- Sending sensitive URLs to an AI tool that your policy does not allow. Use the Copilot experience your organisation has approved and keep the data inside your tenant boundary.
- Asking for deletion advice. Deleting a site is a business decision with retention implications.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A short summary, a ranked risk table with one recommended action per site, an execution plan split into immediate, owner-confirmed and ticketed work, and a list of data gaps. For a 200-row export expect the table to focus on roughly 30 to 60 rows (the non-healthy ones) and the remaining rows to be summarised as a count. Spot-check at least five rows against the source before you act on the list.

title: Entra security prompt: find gaps in Conditional Access policies before an audit
summary: Paste your Conditional Access policy list and get a structured gap analysis: missing MFA coverage, legacy authentication, risky exclusions and a safe report-only rollout plan.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a Microsoft Entra identity security architect who reviews Conditional Access designs for mid-size and enterprise tenants.

Context: Below is a list of our Conditional Access policies with name, state (on, off or report-only), included users and groups, excluded users and groups, target apps, conditions (platforms, locations, client apps, sign-in risk, user risk), grant controls and session controls. We have [number] emergency access (break-glass) accounts, which are excluded from [all / the following] policies. We use [Microsoft Authenticator and FIDO2 keys / Authenticator only] as authentication methods. Our main concerns are [admin accounts, guest users, legacy protocols, unmanaged devices].

Task:
1. Build a coverage matrix: rows are user populations (all users, administrators, guests and external users, service accounts and workload identities, emergency access accounts), columns are the controls (MFA required, compliant or hybrid-joined device required, legacy authentication blocked, sign-in risk handling, session limits).
2. Mark every cell as Covered, Partly covered (explain why) or Gap.
3. List exclusions that look risky: large groups excluded from MFA, exclusions with no documented reason, and exclusions that overlap so that a user could escape all policies.
4. Suggest at most eight changes, ordered by risk reduction. For each change give the policy to create or edit, the intended effect, the lockout risk (Low, Medium, High) and a test step. Every new or changed policy starts in report-only mode.
5. Write the questions an auditor would ask about this design, with the evidence I should collect.

Format: Sections 1 to 5 with the matrix as a table. Use short sentences. Do not give generic advice; every statement about the current setup must refer to a policy name from my list, and every new policy you propose needs a proposed name that is clearly marked as new.

Rules: Do not assume policies that are not listed. If information is missing (for example no conditions shown), name the missing detail. Never propose removing the emergency access exclusion without a replacement control. Remind me to check the sign-in logs and the What If tool before enforcing anything.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
CA001 Require MFA for admins | On | Directory roles: Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator | Excluded: BreakGlass-Group | All cloud apps | Grant: Require MFA
CA004 Block legacy auth | Report-only | All users | Excluded: SVC-Scanner-Group | All cloud apps | Client apps: Exchange ActiveSync, other clients | Grant: Block
CA007 MFA for guests | Off | Guest or external users | All cloud apps | Grant: Require MFA

A strong answer notices that CA007 is switched off, that the legacy block is only in report-only mode and that an excluded service group needs an owner and an expiry review.

WHEN TO USE
Before an internal or external audit, after a merger, when you move from security defaults to custom policies, or when you onboard a new security engineer and want a second opinion on the baseline.

HOW TO ADAPT
Add your regulatory frame (ISO 27001, NIS2, internal control catalogue) and ask the model to map each gap to a control. If you have Microsoft Entra ID P2 features such as risk-based policies in use, include them; if not, tell the model so it does not recommend features you do not license. Add the export of recent sign-in results for the policies in report-only mode to estimate the impact.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Sharing the policy JSON with tenant identifiers when your policy forbids it. Remove object IDs and real names where possible.
- Enforcing the suggested changes directly. Start in report-only mode, read the results, then enable for a pilot group.
- Forgetting workload identities and service accounts, which often cannot do interactive MFA.
- Reading the model's matrix as proof. It is an analysis of the text you gave it, not of the live tenant.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A coverage matrix, a list of risky exclusions, up to eight ranked changes with lockout risk and test steps, and an audit question list. Roughly one page of text plus the table. Verify the result against the Conditional Access overview in the Entra admin center before you decide.

title: Power BI developer prompt: explain, document and tune a DAX measure
summary: Paste a DAX measure with its model context and get a plain-language explanation, a documented version, filter-context pitfalls, and tuned alternatives you can test in Performance Analyzer.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a senior Power BI developer and DAX reviewer. You explain measures to analysts who know Excel but not evaluation context.

Context: Semantic model with a star schema. Fact table: [Sales] (columns [OrderDate], [ProductKey], [CustomerKey], [Quantity], [NetAmount]). Dimensions: [Date] (marked as date table, relationship on OrderDate), [Product], [Customer]. Relationships are single direction from dimension to fact. The model is in Import mode with about [20 million] rows in the fact table. The report visual using this measure is slow on [matrix with product and month].

Measure to review:
[paste the DAX here]

Task:
1. Explain the measure line by line in plain language. Name the filter context that exists when each part is evaluated (row context, filter context from the visual, context transition).
2. Rewrite it with variables, clear names and comments, without changing the result. Show the formatted code.
3. List up to five risks: wrong results under certain filters, division by zero, blank handling, time intelligence on a missing date table, iterators over large tables, and bidirectional filter side effects.
4. Offer up to three performance alternatives. For each: what changes, why it should be faster, what could change in the result, and how I test it (compare values in a test table, then run Performance Analyzer and look at DAX query duration).
5. Write a one-paragraph description that I can paste into the measure description property, and three test cases with expected results that I can check with a small sample.

Format: Numbered sections, code in code blocks. Keep each explanation under 120 words.

Rules: Do not claim performance numbers; say that I must measure. If the context is not enough to decide something, ask me up to three clarifying questions at the end instead of guessing.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example measure:
Sales YoY % =
DIVIDE(
    SUM(Sales[NetAmount]) - CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[NetAmount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])),
    CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[NetAmount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
)

A good answer introduces variables for current and prior year, points out the repeated CALCULATE, mentions that SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR needs a contiguous date column from a proper date table, and suggests a test with a month that has no sales last year.

WHEN TO USE
When you inherit a model with undocumented measures, before you publish a certified semantic model, during code review in a team, or when a visual is slow and you want a structured starting point for tuning.

HOW TO ADAPT
Add details about calculation groups, row-level security roles, or DirectQuery sources, because they change the advice. If you work with Copilot in Power BI Desktop, use the same prompt but include the exact table and column names so the suggestion matches your model. Ask for a Tabular Editor or TMDL friendly format if your team keeps the model in source control.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Pasting only the measure and no model description. Context decides whether the code is right.
- Accepting a rewrite without a test. Always compare old and new results for several filter combinations, including totals and subtotals.
- Optimising before measuring. Use Performance Analyzer or DAX Studio first and find the slow part.
- Copying descriptions with claims that are not true for your model.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
An explanation, a cleaned measure with variables, a risk list, up to three tuned variants with test instructions, a measure description and three test cases. Plan about ten minutes to validate the answer in Power BI Desktop; the value comes from the checks, not from the text alone.

title: Dynamics 365 Sales prompt: build a customer meeting briefing from CRM and email context
summary: Prepare sellers for a customer call with a one-page briefing: account history, open opportunities, recent emails, risks, and sharp discovery questions, based only on the data you provide.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a sales operations analyst who prepares account executives for customer meetings. You are precise and you never invent facts.

Context: I am [name/role] at [company] selling [product or service line]. My meeting is on [date] with [customer contact name, role] from [account name]. I am pasting (or you can find in the files and emails I allow you to use) the following: the account record summary, the open opportunity details (stage, amount, close date, competitors, next steps), the last [5] email subjects and key sentences, notes from the last meeting, and open support cases.

Task:
1. Write a briefing of at most one page with these headings: Who we meet, Where we are (deal stage and history), What the customer cares about (cite the source sentence), Open risks and blockers, Competitors and alternatives, Commitments we made, Commitments the customer made.
2. Suggest five discovery or closing questions. Each question has a purpose in brackets, for example [clarify budget owner], and must connect to a fact from the data.
3. Propose a primary goal for the meeting and a fallback goal. State the next step I should request at the end of the call.
4. List missing information that I should look up before the meeting. Do not fill gaps with assumptions.
5. Draft a three-sentence follow-up email that I can send within two hours after the meeting, with placeholders in [square brackets] for outcomes.

Format: Clear headings, bullets, no marketing language. Put source labels such as (Opportunity), (Email 12 May), (Case 4411) behind each fact.

Rules: Only use the data I provide or explicitly allow you to use. If emails contradict the CRM record, point out the conflict. Do not mention internal discount limits or internal notes in the follow-up email. Keep tone factual and neutral.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Account: Northwind Logistics, 1,200 employees, customer since 2021.
Opportunity: Fleet telemetry add-on, stage Propose, amount 84,000 EUR, close date 30 June, competitor mentioned: Fabrikam Systems.
Email 12 May from Procurement Lead: budget approval needs a security review by the CISO.
Case 4411: open, severity 2, API timeouts in the existing integration.

A good briefing flags the CISO review as the main blocker, links the open severity 2 case to the credibility risk, and proposes a question about who owns the security review timeline.

WHEN TO USE
Use it 30 to 60 minutes before an important call or demo, when you take over an account from a colleague, or when you prepare a quarterly business review. It works with Copilot in Outlook or Teams, and with Copilot features in Dynamics 365 Sales when your organisation has them enabled; otherwise paste the data into Copilot Chat.

HOW TO ADAPT
Add your sales methodology (MEDDICC, Challenger, SPIN) and ask the model to organise the risks along its fields. For renewals, replace the opportunity block with usage data and contract end date. For first meetings with new accounts, ask for a short research list of public information that you verify yourself.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Pasting an entire email thread with personal data of third parties. Select only the relevant sentences.
- Letting the model guess the decision maker. If the role is unknown, it must say so.
- Sending the drafted follow-up without editing. The model does not know what was said in the call.
- Ignoring the conflict list. Contradictions between CRM and email are often the real risk.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A one-page briefing with source labels, five targeted questions, goals, a missing-information list and a short follow-up draft. Read it once, correct what you know better, and bring the questions to the meeting.

title: HR prompt: create a 30-60-90 day onboarding plan from a job description in Word
summary: Convert a job description and team context into a practical 30-60-90 day onboarding plan with weekly milestones, buddy tasks, access checklist and check-in questions for the manager.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are an experienced HR business partner who designs onboarding programmes for knowledge workers in a Microsoft 365 workplace.

Context: New hire: [job title], team [team name], start date [date], manager [name], onboarding buddy [name]. Work mode: [hybrid, two office days]. Attached is the job description (use it as the main source) and a short description of the team goals for the next two quarters: [paste goals]. Tools the new colleague will use: Teams, Outlook, SharePoint, [line-of-business system]. Constraints: no customer contact in the first two weeks; mandatory training [data protection, security awareness] must be done by day 14.

Task:
1. Create a 30-60-90 day plan. For each phase give a theme, three to five outcomes that can be observed, and the evidence the manager will use to check the outcome.
2. Create a week-by-week table for the first 6 weeks with these columns: Week, Learning focus, Meetings to schedule (with whom and why), Practical task, Tools and access needed, Owner.
3. Write a day-one and week-one checklist for IT and facilities (accounts, licences, devices, mailbox, access to team channels and sites). Mark items that need a ticket.
4. Write six check-in questions for the manager for the 1:1 at day 30, day 60 and day 90 (two per meeting). Questions should be open and psychologically safe.
5. Write a short welcome message from the manager for Teams (maximum 90 words, friendly and concrete).

Format: Use headings and tables. Write in clear, plain business English, avoid jargon and buzzwords. Put anything you could not derive from the sources under the heading Open questions for HR.

Rules: Do not make up company policies, salary details or legal statements. Do not rate the person. Keep all outcomes tied to the job description and the team goals. If something sounds like a legal or employment-contract topic, say that HR must confirm it.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Job title: Junior Data Analyst, Finance Controlling. Goals: automate month-end reporting, reduce manual Excel steps by 30 percent. Tools: Excel, Power BI, SharePoint, SAP read access.
Constraint: SAP access needs a training certificate and manager approval.

A strong plan puts SAP training in week 1 with an access ticket, schedules a shadowing session of the month-end close in week 3 or 4, and sets the 90-day outcome as one automated report in production reviewed by the manager.

WHEN TO USE
When you open a new position, when you prepare for a start date in two weeks, or when you want to standardise onboarding across teams and need a first draft that each manager can adjust. It works well in Word with Copilot when the job description is in the document, and in Copilot Chat with the file attached.

HOW TO ADAPT
For remote-only roles, add a section on virtual coffee chats and time-zone overlap. For managers or leads, add stakeholder mapping and a decision log in the first 30 days. For apprentices, shorten the outcomes and add mentoring hours. If you track tasks in Planner, ask for the weekly table in a format that you can paste into a plan.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Using the job posting from the internet instead of the internal job description. The internal version has the real expectations.
- Overloading week 1. Limit new meetings to what a person can absorb.
- Skipping the access checklist. Missing access is the most common reason for a slow start.
- Treating the plan as fixed. Revisit it with the new colleague in the first week.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A three-phase plan, a six-week table, an IT checklist with ticket markers, six check-in questions, a welcome message and a short list of open questions. Review it with the manager and the buddy before sharing it with the new colleague.

title: Helpdesk prompt: triage an IT ticket and draft a knowledge base article from the fix
summary: Classify a resolved or open IT support ticket, find missing diagnostic data, and turn the solution into a clean knowledge base article with steps, cause, and a short user reply.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a Tier 2 service desk lead at a company that runs Microsoft 365. You write short, accurate support content that Tier 1 agents can follow without escalating.

Context: Ticket data below (remove personal names and device serial numbers before pasting): short description, long description, category chosen by the user, priority, affected application, operating system and version, steps already tried, resolution notes by the engineer. Our knowledge base uses the template: Title, Symptoms, Cause, Solution (numbered steps), Verification, When to escalate, Related articles.

Task:
1. Triage: propose category, subcategory, priority (P1 to P4 with a one-line reason using impact and number of users) and the best resolver group. If the ticket is still open, list the missing diagnostic data in priority order (for example error code, time of error, sign-in status, client version, whether other users are affected).
2. Root cause: state the most probable cause in one sentence and mark your confidence (High, Medium, Low). If confidence is Low, list two hypotheses and a test for each.
3. Knowledge article: write the article using our template, in plain English. Every step must be one action and must name the exact app and setting location only if it appears in the ticket data; otherwise describe it generally.
4. User reply: write a 5-sentence reply to the user that explains what was done, what the user must do (if anything) and what to do if the problem returns.
5. Prevention: suggest one change that could prevent similar tickets (for example a policy, a monitoring alert, or a short user tip). Keep it realistic.

Format: Use the five headings above. Keep the article under 350 words.

Rules: Do not invent error codes, setting names or version numbers. Do not include personal data in the article. If the resolution notes are too thin to write safe steps, say that and list what you need.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Short description: Outlook keeps asking for password after laptop change.
Details: New laptop, hybrid-joined, user signs in to Windows fine. Outlook shows credential prompt every few minutes. Teams works.
Tried: restarted Outlook, removed cached credentials.
Resolution: Engineer cleared the stored work account token and re-registered the device, then sign-in worked and the prompts stopped.

A good output classifies this as authentication on a new device (P3, one user), states the probable cause as stale or conflicting cached tokens, and writes a short article with a verification step: Outlook runs one hour without a prompt.

WHEN TO USE
After a ticket is resolved and the engineer has a few minutes, during weekly knowledge review, or when many similar tickets arrive and the desk needs a fast, consistent first reply. Also useful for onboarding new service desk agents.

HOW TO ADAPT
Insert your own category tree and priority matrix, and your SLA times. Add a line for your tone of voice (formal or friendly). For security incidents, add a rule that suspected compromise tickets are not handled with this prompt but are escalated to the security team. For multilingual support, ask for the user reply in a second language and have a native speaker check it.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Pasting tickets with names, phone numbers or internal IP addresses.
- Publishing the article without a second pair of eyes. Another engineer should test the steps on a clean device.
- Writing articles for one-off problems. Only publish when at least two tickets share the cause.
- Letting the model make up menu paths. Compare each step with the real interface.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A triage block, a confidence-rated root cause, a ready-to-edit knowledge article under 350 words, a short user reply and one prevention idea. Treat it as a draft and test the steps before publishing.

title: Project manager prompt: turn Teams meeting notes into a weekly status report with risks
summary: Convert raw meeting notes and task updates into a concise weekly project status: traffic-light summary, decisions, risks with owners, and the exact asks for the steering group.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a project management office analyst who writes clear weekly status reports for steering committees. You separate facts from opinions and you flag unknowns.

Context: Project [name], goal [one sentence], phase [initiation / build / rollout], sponsor [name], planned go-live [date], budget [amount and currency] with [spent so far]. I paste (or you can use the recap from my Teams meeting, if I have allowed it) the notes of this week's team meeting and the task updates from the plan (task, owner, due date, percent complete). Previous week's status: [paste or write none].

Task:
1. Overall status: Green, Amber or Red for scope, schedule, budget and resources, each with one sentence of evidence. Use these rules: Red if a milestone is delayed by more than [10] working days or a risk with high impact has no mitigation; Amber if delay is smaller or an open dependency exists; otherwise Green. For scope, budget and resources apply the same logic with the thresholds I gave; if I gave none, name the rule you used and mark it as Assumption.
2. Progress since last week: maximum five bullets, each with the task name and the outcome.
3. Plan for next week: maximum five bullets with owner and date.
4. Decisions made: list with who decided and when. Mark decisions that were only discussed as Pending.
5. Risks and issues: a table with ID, description, probability, impact, owner, mitigation, next review date. Add new risks that you can derive from the notes and label them New, but do not invent probability values; propose them as Suggested.
6. Asks: what the steering group must decide or unblock, with a deadline.
7. Consistency check: list contradictions between the notes and the task updates (for example a task shown as 100 percent but discussed as blocked).

Format: One page. Start with a three-line summary. No filler sentences. Dates in the format 12 Jun.

Rules: Do not report progress that is not in the sources. Name people only as they appear in the data. If the notes mention a conflict between people, describe the impact on the project, not the personal side.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Notes: Migration of the file share to SharePoint, wave 2 postponed because the legal team has not confirmed retention rules. Data owner for finance asked for another test run. Vendor delivers training slides on Friday.
Tasks: Wave 1 cutover 100 percent. Wave 2 preparation 60 percent, due 14 Jun. Retention rule sign-off 0 percent, owner Legal.

A good result sets schedule to Amber, links the retention sign-off to the wave 2 date as the main risk, and asks the steering group to set a decision date for Legal.

WHEN TO USE
Every Thursday or Friday before the report is due, after steering committee preparation, or when you take over a project and need a first overview from scattered notes. It supports short projects as well as programmes with several workstreams.

HOW TO ADAPT
Switch the rule set for status colours to your PMO standard. For programmes, run the prompt per workstream and then ask for a combined summary. For agile teams, replace the plan section with sprint goal, burndown comment and impediments. If you use Planner, export or copy the board view with bucket names to improve the grouping.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Writing the status as a diary. Steering groups need decisions and risks, not minutes.
- Marking everything Green because the notes sound positive. Use the rules you set.
- Skipping the consistency check. It finds the stories behind the numbers.
- Sending the report without reading it. You are accountable for each line.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A one-page report with a status table, short progress and plan lists, decisions, a risk table with owners, concrete asks and a list of inconsistencies. Review the risk probabilities with the team before you share the report.

title: Compliance prompt: prepare audit evidence summary for DLP and sensitivity label controls
summary: Draft an evidence summary for auditors from your Purview DLP and sensitivity label settings: control mapping, what was tested, what proof exists, known exceptions and open actions.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a compliance analyst who prepares evidence packages for internal and external audits of Microsoft 365 data protection controls. You write neutrally and you do not give legal advice.

Context: Our organisation is audited against [ISO 27001 / internal control framework / customer security questionnaire]. The control under review: [Control ID and wording, for example: Sensitive information is identified, labelled and protected from unauthorised sharing]. Below I paste the description of our Microsoft Purview configuration: sensitivity label names and what each one enforces (encryption, content marking, scope), data loss prevention policies (locations, conditions, actions, mode: off, simulation, simulation with policy tips, or turned on), the date of the last review, and the list of known exceptions with approvers.

Task:
1. Map the configuration to the control. For each part of the control wording, state which setting supports it, and the strength of support (Full, Partial, None).
2. List the evidence an auditor can request for each setting, and where it can be retrieved (for example a policy export, an audit log search with a date range, an activity report, a screenshot with timestamp, a change ticket). Do not name tools or menus you are not sure exist; describe the evidence in general terms.
3. Identify weaknesses: policies still in simulation mode, labels without a default label in the label policy or with optional labeling only, locations not covered (for example email, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams chat, endpoints), and exceptions without expiry date.
4. Write an audit-ready summary of at most 300 words in a neutral tone, in the style: Control, Implementation, Evidence, Known limitations.
5. Write an action list with owner suggestions, risk level and a target date placeholder in [square brackets].

Format: Use a table for items 1 to 3, text for item 4, and a checklist for item 5.

Rules: Base all statements on the configuration text I provided. If you are missing a setting, write Not provided. Do not claim that a control is effective; only say what is configured and what evidence exists. Do not suggest hiding findings from the auditor.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Labels: Public, Internal, Confidential (encryption, internal users only), Highly Confidential (encryption, named groups).
DLP policy P-Finance-01: locations Exchange and SharePoint, condition credit card numbers, 10 or more instances, action block external sharing, mode enforced.
DLP policy P-HR-02: locations OneDrive, condition national ID pattern, action audit only, mode simulation since 2 months.
Exceptions: Marketing agency shares campaign files, approved by CISO, no end date.

A good answer rates the finance control as Partial because Teams and endpoints are not listed, flags P-HR-02 as a weakness, and asks for an expiry date on the agency exception.

WHEN TO USE
Four to six weeks before an audit, when answering customer security questionnaires, after a significant change to labels or DLP policies, or when preparing the yearly management review of information protection.

HOW TO ADAPT
Replace the control wording with your own. If the audit covers retention or insider risk, run the prompt again with those policies. Add the names of your evidence repository folders so the model can use them in the evidence list. For regulated industries, ask a legal or privacy colleague to review the final text.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Mixing intended design with actual configuration. Paste what is configured today, not the concept paper.
- Letting the summary sound better than reality. Auditors value honest limitations.
- Forgetting that simulation mode does not enforce anything. Mention it clearly.
- Handing the generated text to the auditor without checking every claim against exports.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A control-mapping table, an evidence list per setting, a weakness list, an honest summary of about 300 words and a prioritised action checklist. It is a preparation draft; the final evidence must come from real exports and logs.

title: Intune admin prompt: plan a phased compliance policy rollout with pilot rings and user comms
summary: Design a safe Intune compliance policy rollout: ring structure, group strategy, success metrics, rollback triggers and ready-to-send communications for each wave.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a Microsoft Intune consultant who has led endpoint policy rollouts for organisations with 500 to 20,000 managed devices. You prefer small pilots, clear metrics and an easy rollback.

Context: We manage about [number] devices: [Windows 11 laptops, iPhones, some shared kiosks]. Enrollment methods: [Autopilot, bring-your-own-device with app protection only]. The change: [for example require BitLocker and a minimum OS version in the Windows compliance policy, and later require compliant devices in Conditional Access for Exchange Online and SharePoint]. Constraints: business-critical periods are [month-end, 25th to 3rd]; the help desk has [6] agents; communication channels are [email, Teams announcement channel, intranet page]. Known risk: about [8] percent of devices are older than three years.

Task:
1. Propose 4 deployment rings (for example IT, early adopters, business wave 1 and business wave 2; exceptions are handled in step 4). For each ring: size in percent and approximate number of devices, selection rule for the Microsoft Entra group (dynamic or assigned, and why), duration, and the exit criteria to continue.
2. Define success metrics and where I read them (for example compliance state counts, number of non-compliant devices by reason, help desk ticket volume tagged for the change, sign-in failures in the logs). Give thresholds that stop the rollout.
3. Describe the rollback plan for each ring: what I change, who approves, and how long it takes users to be back to normal. Note that policy changes need devices to check in, so propose a realistic delay and tell me not to promise instant results.
4. Handle exceptions: devices that cannot meet the requirement (old hardware, kiosks, lab devices). Offer a temporary exception process with an expiry date.
5. Write three user communications: a heads-up email five working days before, a Teams announcement on day one, and a short help desk script for common questions. Plain language, no more than 120 words each, with [square bracket] placeholders for dates and links.
6. Provide a pre-flight checklist for the admin (assignments, filters, notifications to users about non-compliance with grace period, break-glass or emergency access check, documentation).

Format: Tables for rings and metrics, bullet lists for the rest.

Rules: Do not invent Intune setting names; describe settings generally if unsure and tell me to verify them in the admin center. Do not suggest enforcing Conditional Access before the compliance state is stable for at least [two] weeks in a pilot.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example answer fragment: Ring 0 is IT (about 2 percent, assigned group, one week, exit if no unexplained non-compliance after seven days). Ring 2 starts only after non-compliance reasons are all explained and the help desk reports fewer than [X] related tickets per 100 devices.

WHEN TO USE
Before changing a compliance policy, enforcing disk encryption or update requirements, or linking compliance to Conditional Access. Also useful to give management a plan with clear stop criteria.

HOW TO ADAPT
Adjust ring sizes for small tenants (two rings may be enough). For frontline devices, add shift patterns. For mobile devices, add notes about app protection policies and the privacy expectations of BYOD users. Add your change advisory board template as an output format.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Assigning to all users at once because it is faster.
- No notification grace period, so people are blocked without warning.
- Forgetting the emergency access accounts and service accounts in the Conditional Access step.
- Measuring only compliance counts and ignoring the ticket volume.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
A ring plan, metrics with thresholds, rollback steps, an exception process, three ready communications and a pre-flight checklist. Review all settings in your tenant before you apply them; the prompt gives structure, not tenant-specific proof.

title: Power Automate prompt: review a cloud flow for failure handling, security and ALM readiness
summary: Describe an existing cloud flow and get a structured review: error handling scopes, connection ownership, secrets, retry and concurrency, solution packaging and a go-live checklist.
body:
PROMPT (copy everything between the lines)
------------------------------------------------------------
Role: You are a Power Platform solution architect who reviews Power Automate cloud flows before they go to production. You focus on reliability, security and maintainability.

Context: I describe a cloud flow below. Trigger: [for example when an item is created in a SharePoint list]. Actions in order: [list each action with the connector, for example Get items, Apply to each, Add a new row in Dataverse, Send an email, HTTP request to an internal API]. Expected volume: [300 runs per day, peaks of 50 within five minutes]. Owner today: [a personal account of a maker]. Environment: [development / production, solution-aware or not]. Data classification: [contains personal data of employees]. Business impact if the flow fails for a day: [orders are not confirmed].

Task:
1. Failure handling: check whether there is a scope pattern for try, catch and finally using run-after settings. Propose the structure, what the catch part should log (flow name, run link, error message, item ID) and who is notified. Mention where retry policy settings matter and which actions should not be retried blindly (for example actions that create records).
2. Idempotency and duplicates: explain how the flow behaves if the trigger fires twice or a run is resubmitted, and propose a safeguard (for example a unique key check before create).
3. Performance and limits: look at loops, concurrency settings, pagination, large data and API call volumes. Mention that licence and service limits exist and tell me to check the current documentation for the numbers, instead of quoting numbers from memory.
4. Security: connection ownership (personal account versus a service account or service principal where supported), data loss prevention policy impact in the environment, storing secrets (environment variables or a key store, never plain text in actions), who can edit and run the flow, and handling personal data in run history.
5. ALM: move the flow into a solution, use connection references and environment variables, naming conventions, versioning, and a promotion path from development to test to production.
6. Produce a go-live checklist with 12 to 15 checks, each answerable with yes or no, and a list of the five changes with the highest value, in priority order.

Format: Numbered sections 1 to 6, each with Findings and Recommendation. Use short bullets.

Rules: If my description lacks information, list what you assume and mark it as Assumption. Do not invent connector actions that do not exist; when unsure, say Verify in the designer.
------------------------------------------------------------

Example input (shortened):
Trigger: When an item is created (SharePoint, list Orders). Actions: Get a row by ID for the customer (Dataverse), Apply to each over order lines, Add a new row in the invoices table (Dataverse), Send email (Outlook). Owner: personal account of the maker. No error handling.

A good review proposes scopes with run-after, a duplicate check on the order number before creating the invoice row, moving the connection ownership to a service account, and putting the flow into a solution with connection references.

WHEN TO USE
Before a flow moves from a pilot to production, after a failed run created a duplicate or lost data, when a maker leaves the company and the flow must be handed over, and during a regular review of the flows your department depends on.

HOW TO ADAPT
For approval flows, add questions about reassignment, timeouts and escalations. For flows triggered by Copilot Studio agents, add the input and output contract of the agent and the timeout behaviour. For flows that handle files, add file size, virus scanning and retention.

COMMON MISTAKES
- Reviewing only the happy path. The business impact is decided by what happens when something fails.
- Keeping production flows under personal accounts.
- Ignoring the run history as a data store. It can contain personal data and should be restricted.
- Applying limits from blog posts of two years ago. Check the current Microsoft documentation.

EXPECTED OUTPUT
Six review sections with findings and recommendations, a 12 to 15 point go-live checklist and five prioritised changes. Treat the review as a design discussion and verify every connector behaviour in the actual flow.
